title: Book 3, Chapter 9 — Fourth and Fifth Years of the War—Revolt of Mitylene
paragraphs: The next summer, just as the corn was getting ripe, the Peloponnesians and their allies invaded Attica under the command of Archidamus, son of Zeuxidamus, king of the Lacedaemonians, and sat down and ravaged the country. The Athenian horse, as usual, attacked them wherever it was practicable and prevented the mass of the light troops from advancing from camp and damaging the parts near the city. After staying for as long as their provisions allowed, the invaders withdrew and dispersed to their several cities.

Immediately after the Peloponnesian invasion, all of Lesbos except Methymna revolted from the Athenians. The Lesbians had wished to revolt even before the war, but the Lacedaemonians would not receive them; and even now, when they did revolt, they were forced to do so sooner than they had intended. They were waiting until the moles for their harbours, and the ships and walls under construction, should be finished, and for the arrival of archers, corn, and other things they were fetching from the Pontus. But the Tenedians, with whom they were at enmity, the Methymnians, and certain factious men in Mitylene itself who were proxenoi of Athens, informed the Athenians that the Mitylenians were forcibly uniting the island under their rule, and that the preparations they were so busy with had all been concerted with the Boeotians—their kindred—and with the Lacedaemonians, with a view to revolt; and that unless the Athenians intervened at once, Athens would lose Lesbos.

However, the Athenians, exhausted by the plague and by the war that had recently broken out and was now raging, thought it a serious matter to add Lesbos, with its fleet and untouched resources, to the list of their enemies. At first they refused to believe the charge, giving too much weight to their wish that it might not be true. But when an embassy they sent failed to persuade the Mitylenians to give up the union and the preparations complained of, they grew alarmed and resolved to strike the first blow. They suddenly sent off forty ships that had been got ready to sail round the Peloponnese, under the command of Cleippides, son of Deinias, and two others. They had been told of a festival in honour of the Malean Apollo outside the town, which the whole people of Mitylene celebrated, and at which, if they made haste, they might hope to take them by surprise. If the plan succeeded, well and good; if not, they were to order the Mitylenians to hand over their ships and pull down their walls, and if they refused, declare war. The ships set out. The ten galleys forming the Mitylenian contingent serving with the fleet under the terms of the alliance were detained by the Athenians, and their crews placed in custody. The Mitylenians, however, were informed of the expedition by a man who crossed from Athens to Euboea, went overland to Geraestus, and from there sailed in a merchantman he found about to put to sea, reaching Mitylene on the third day after leaving Athens. The Mitylenians accordingly stayed away from the temple at Malea, and barricaded and kept guard around the half-finished portions of their walls and harbours.

When the Athenians sailed in not long afterwards and saw how things stood, the generals delivered their orders, and on the Mitylenians’ refusal to obey, opened hostilities. The Mitylenians, thus forced to go to war without warning and unprepared, at first sailed out with their fleet and made some show of fighting, a little in front of the harbour. But driven back by the Athenian ships, they immediately offered to negotiate with the commanders, hoping if possible to get the Athenian fleet away for the moment on any tolerable terms. The Athenian commanders accepted their offers, themselves fearing they might not be able to cope with the whole of Lesbos. An armistice was concluded, and the Mitylenians sent to Athens one of the informers, already repenting of his conduct, along with others, to try to persuade the Athenians of the innocence of their intentions and to get the fleet recalled. Meanwhile, having no great hope of a favourable answer from Athens, they also sent off a galley with envoys to Lacedaemon, unobserved by the Athenian fleet anchored at Malea to the north of the town.

While these envoys, having reached Lacedaemon after a difficult journey across the open sea, were negotiating for help to be sent them, the ambassadors from Athens returned having achieved nothing. Hostilities were at once begun by the Mitylenians and the rest of Lesbos—except for the Methymnians, who came to the aid of the Athenians along with the Imbrians and Lemnians and a few of the other allies. The Mitylenians made a sortie with all their forces against the Athenian camp; and a battle ensued, in which they gained some slight advantage, but withdrew nonetheless, not feeling confident enough to spend the night in the field. After this they kept quiet, wishing to wait for the chance of reinforcements arriving from the Peloponnese before making a second venture. They were encouraged by the arrival of Meleas, a Laconian, and Hermaeondas, a Theban, who had been sent off before the insurrection but had not been able to reach Lesbos before the Athenian expedition. They now slipped in by galley after the battle and advised them to send another galley and envoys back with them, which the Mitylenians accordingly did.

Meanwhile the Athenians, greatly encouraged by the inactivity of the Mitylenians, summoned allies to their aid—who came in all the more readily for seeing so little vigour from the Lesbians. Bringing their ships round to a new station south of the town, they fortified two camps, one on each side of the city, and instituted a blockade of both harbours. The sea was thus closed against the Mitylenians, who, however, commanded the whole country, along with the rest of the Lesbians who had now joined them. The Athenians held only a limited area around their camps, using Malea more as the station for their ships and their market.

While the war continued in this way at Mitylene, about the same time that summer the Athenians also sent thirty ships to the Peloponnese under Asopius, son of Phormio. The Acarnanians had insisted that the commander sent should be some son or relative of Phormio. As the ships coasted along, they ravaged the seaboard of Laconia. After this, Asopius sent most of the fleet home and went on with twelve vessels to Naupactus, and afterwards, raising the whole Acarnanian population, made an expedition against Oeniadae, the fleet sailing along the Achelous while the army laid waste the country. The inhabitants, however, showing no signs of submitting, he dismissed the land forces and himself sailed to Leucas. Making a descent on Nericus, he was cut off during his retreat, with most of his troops, by the local people aided by some coastguards. After this the Athenians sailed away, recovering their dead from the Leucadians under truce.

Meanwhile the envoys of the Mitylenians sent out in the first ship were told by the Lacedaemonians to come to Olympia, so that the rest of the allies might hear them and decide on their case, and so they journeyed there. It was the Olympiad in which the Rhodian Dorieus won his second victory, and the envoys, having been introduced to make their speech after the festival, spoke as follows:

“Lacedaemonians and allies, the rule established among the Hellenes is not unknown to us. Those who revolt in war and forsake their former confederacy are favourably regarded by those who receive them, in so far as they are useful, but otherwise are thought less well of, since they are considered traitors to their former friends. Nor is this an unfair way of judging, where rebels and the power they secede from are at one in policy and sympathy, are matched in resources and power, and where no reasonable ground for the rebellion exists. But with us and the Athenians this was not the case; and no one need think the worse of us for revolting from them in danger, after having been honoured by them in time of peace.

“Justice and honesty will be the first topics of our speech, especially as we are asking for alliance. We know that there can never be any solid friendship between individuals, or any worthwhile union between communities, unless the parties are persuaded of each other’s honesty and are generally congenial to one another, since difference of feeling produces difference of conduct. Between ourselves and the Athenians, alliance began when you withdrew from the Median War and they remained to finish the business. But we did not become allies of the Athenians for the subjugation of the Hellenes; we became allies of the Hellenes for their liberation from the Mede. As long as the Athenians led us fairly, we followed them loyally; but when we saw them relax their hostility to the Mede and try to compass the subjection of the allies, our apprehensions began. Unable, however, to unite and defend themselves on account of the number of confederates that had votes, all the allies were enslaved, except ourselves and the Chians, who continued to send our contingents as independent and nominally free states. But we could no longer feel any trust in Athens as a leader, judging by the examples already given; it was unlikely that she would reduce our fellow confederates and not do the same to us, the only ones left, whenever she had the power.

“Had all of us still been independent, we could have had more faith in their not attempting any change. But with most being their subjects while they treated us as equals, they would naturally chafe at this solitary instance of independence set against the submission of the majority, especially as they grew daily more powerful and we more isolated. The only sound basis for an alliance is for each party to be equally afraid of the other; he who would like to encroach is then deterred by the reflection that he will not have the odds in his favour. Again, if we were left independent, it was only because they thought they saw their way to empire more clearly through specious language and political paths than by force. Not only were we useful as evidence that powers who had votes, like themselves, would surely not join in their expeditions against their will, without the party attacked being in the wrong; but the same system also enabled them to lead the stronger states against the weaker first, and so to leave the strongest for last, stripped of their natural allies and less capable of resistance. Had they begun with us, while all the states still controlled their own resources and there was a centre to rally around, the work of subjugation would have been less easy. Besides this, our navy gave them some apprehension: it was always possible that it might unite with you or with some other power and become dangerous to Athens. The court we paid to their popular party and its leaders for the time being also helped us to maintain our independence. We did not expect, however, to be able to do so much longer, if this war had not broken out, given the examples we had seen of their conduct toward the rest.

“How then could we put any trust in such friendship or freedom as we had here? We accepted each other against our inclination; fear made them court us in war, and us them in peace; sympathy, the ordinary basis of confidence, was replaced by terror, fear having more share than friendship in keeping us in the alliance. The first party that should be encouraged by the hope of impunity was certain to break faith with the other. So to condemn us for being the first to break off—because they delay the blow we dread, instead of waiting ourselves to know for certain whether it will be dealt or not—is to take a false view of the case. If we were equally able to meet their plots and imitate their delay, we would be their equals and would be under no necessity of being their subjects; but since the liberty of attacking is always theirs, the liberty of defending should clearly be ours.

“Such, Lacedaemonians and allies, are the grounds and reasons for our revolt—clear enough to convince our hearers of the fairness of our conduct, and sufficient to alarm us and make us turn to some means of safety. We wished to do this long ago, when we sent to you on the subject while the peace still held, but were thwarted by your refusal to receive us. Now, when the Boeotians invited us, we at once responded to the call, and decided on a twofold revolt—from the Hellenes and from the Athenians: not to help the latter in harming the former, but to join in their liberation; not to allow the Athenians in the end to destroy us, but to act against them in time. Our revolt, however, has taken place prematurely and without preparation—a fact that makes it all the more incumbent on you to receive us into alliance and send us speedy relief, in order to show that you support your friends, and at the same time harm your enemies. You have an opportunity such as you never had before. Disease and expenditure have wasted the Athenians: their ships are either cruising round your coasts or engaged in blockading us; and they will not likely have any to spare, if you invade them a second time this summer by sea and land. Either they will offer no resistance to your vessels, or they will withdraw from both our shores. Nor must you think this is a case of putting yourselves in danger for a country which is not yours. Lesbos may seem far off, but when help is wanted she will be found near enough. The war will not be decided in Attica, as some imagine, but in the countries that support Attica; the Athenian revenue is drawn from her allies, and will become still larger if they reduce us, since not only will no other state revolt, but our resources will be added to theirs, and we shall be treated worse than those that were enslaved before. But if you support us frankly, you will add to your side a state with a large navy—your great want; you will smooth the way to the overthrow of the Athenians by depriving them of their allies, who will be greatly encouraged to come over; and you will free yourselves from the charge laid against you, of failing to support insurrection. In short, only show yourselves as liberators, and you may count on having the advantage in the war.

“Respect, then, the hopes the Hellenes have placed in you, and that Olympian Zeus in whose temple we stand as your suppliants; become the allies and defenders of the Mitylenians, and do not sacrifice us, who put our lives upon the hazard, in a cause whose success will bring general good to all, and whose failure—through your refusing to help us—will bring still more general harm. Be the men the Hellenes think you are, and our fears desire.”

Such were the words of the Mitylenians. After hearing them out, the Lacedaemonians and confederates granted what they urged, took the Lesbians into alliance, and decided in favour of the invasion of Attica. They told the allies present to march as quickly as possible to the Isthmus with two-thirds of their forces; arriving there first themselves, they got ready hauling machines to carry their ships across from Corinth to the sea on the side facing Athens, in order to attack by sea and land at once. However, the zeal they displayed was not matched by the rest of the confederates, who came in slowly, being engaged in harvesting their corn and sick of making expeditions.

Meanwhile the Athenians, aware that the enemy’s preparations were rooted in the conviction of their weakness, and wishing to show him he was mistaken—that they were able, without moving the Lesbian fleet, to repel with ease the one that menaced them from the Peloponnese—manned a hundred ships by embarking the citizens of Athens, except the knights and Pentacosiomedimni, and the resident aliens. Putting out to the Isthmus, they displayed their power and made descents on the Peloponnese wherever they pleased. So glaring a disappointment made the Lacedaemonians think the Lesbians had not spoken the truth. Embarrassed by the non-appearance of the confederates, and by news that the thirty ships round the Peloponnese were ravaging the lands near Sparta, they went back home. Afterwards, however, they prepared a fleet to send to Lesbos, ordering a total of forty ships from the cities in the league, and appointed Alcidas to command the expedition in his capacity of high admiral. The Athenians in the hundred ships, on seeing the Lacedaemonians go home, went home likewise.

If, at the time this fleet was at sea, Athens had nearly the largest number of first-rate ships in commission she ever possessed at any one moment, she had as many or even more when the war began. At that time one hundred guarded Attica, Euboea, and Salamis; another hundred were cruising round the Peloponnese, besides those employed at Potidæa and elsewhere—a grand total of two hundred and fifty vessels on active service in a single summer. This, together with Potidæa, most exhausted her revenues. Potidæa was blockaded by a force of heavy infantry (each drawing two drachmae a day, one for himself and another for his servant), three thousand at first and kept at this number until the end of the siege; besides sixteen hundred under Phormio who left before it was over; and the ships were all paid at the same rate. In this way her money was spent at first, and this was the largest number of ships ever manned by her.

About the same time the Lacedaemonians were at the Isthmus, the Mitylenians marched by land with their mercenaries against Methymna, which they thought to gain by treachery. After assaulting the town and not meeting the success they expected, they withdrew to Antissa, Pyrrha, and Eresus; and taking measures for the better security of these towns and strengthening their walls, hastily returned home. After their departure the Methymnians marched against Antissa, but were defeated in a sortie by the Antissians and their mercenaries, and retreated in haste after losing many of their number. When word of this reached Athens, and the Athenians learned that the Mitylenians were masters of the country and their own soldiers unable to hold them in check, they sent out about the beginning of autumn Paches, son of Epicurus, to take command, with a thousand Athenian heavy infantry; who worked their own passage and, on arriving at Mitylene, built a single wall all round it, with forts erected at some of the strongest points. Mitylene was thus blockaded strictly on both sides, by land and by sea; and winter was now drawing near.

The Athenians, needing money for the siege, although they had for the first time raised a contribution of two hundred talents from their own citizens, now sent out twelve ships to levy subsidies from their allies, with Lysicles and four others in command. After cruising to various places and laying them under contribution, Lysicles went up the country from Myus, in Caria, across the plain of the Meander, as far as the hill of Sandius; and being attacked by the Carians and the people of Anaia, was killed with many of his soldiers.

The same winter the Plataeans, still being besieged by the Peloponnesians and Boeotians, distressed by the failure of their provisions and seeing no hope of relief from Athens or any other means of safety, formed a scheme with the Athenians besieged with them to escape, if possible, by forcing their way over the enemy’s walls. The plan was suggested by Theaenetus, son of Tolmides, a soothsayer, and Eupompides, son of Daimachus, one of their generals. At first all were to take part; afterwards half hung back, thinking the risk too great. About two hundred and twenty, however, voluntarily persisted in the attempt, which was carried out as follows. Ladders were made to match the height of the enemy’s wall, which they measured by the layers of bricks—the side facing them not being thoroughly whitewashed. The bricks were counted by many men at once; some might miss the right number, but most would hit it, especially as they counted over and over again, and were close enough to the wall to see it well enough for their purpose. The length needed for the ladders was thus calculated from the breadth of a brick.

Now the wall of the Peloponnesians was constructed as follows. It consisted of two lines drawn round the place, one against the Plataeans, the other against any attack from outside, from Athens, about sixteen feet apart. The intermediate space of sixteen feet was occupied by huts assigned to the soldiers on guard, built in a single block so as to give the appearance of one thick wall with battlements on either side. At intervals of every ten battlements were towers of considerable size, the same width as the wall, reaching right across from its inner to its outer face, with no way of passing except through the middle. Accordingly, on stormy and wet nights, the battlements were left empty, and guard was kept from the towers, which were not far apart and roofed in above.

Such was the structure of the wall by which the Plataeans were blockaded. When their preparations were complete, they waited for a stormy night of wind and rain, with no moon, and then set out, guided by the authors of the enterprise. First they crossed the ditch that ran round the town; then they reached the enemy’s wall unnoticed by the sentinels, who could not see them in the darkness or hear them, since the wind drowned out the noise of their approach with its roar. They also kept a good distance from one another, so as not to be betrayed by the clash of their weapons. They were lightly equipped, with only the left foot shod, to keep them from slipping in the mud. They came up to the battlements at one of the intermediate spaces where they knew them to be unguarded. The men carrying the ladders went first and planted them; next twelve light-armed soldiers, with only a dagger and a breastplate, mounted, led by Ammias, son of Coroebus, who was the first on the wall; his followers got up after him and went six to each of the towers. After these came another party of light troops armed with spears, whose shields—so that they could climb more easily—were carried by men behind, who would hand them up when they faced the enemy. After a good many had mounted, they were discovered by the sentinels in the towers, by the noise of a tile knocked down by one of the Plataeans as he laid hold of the battlements. The alarm was instantly given, and the troops rushed to the wall, not knowing the nature of the danger because of the dark night and stormy weather. The Plataeans in the town had also chosen that moment to make a sortie against the Peloponnesian wall on the side opposite to where their men were getting over, in order to divert the besiegers’ attention. So the besiegers stayed distracted at their various posts, none venturing to leave his station to give help, and at a loss to guess what was happening. Meanwhile the three hundred set aside for emergencies went outside the wall in the direction of the alarm. Fire-signals of an attack were also raised toward Thebes; but the Plataeans in the town at once displayed a number of others, prepared in advance for this very purpose, in order to render the enemy’s signals unintelligible and to prevent his friends from getting a true picture of what was happening and coming to his aid before their comrades who had gone out had made good their escape and reached safety.

Meanwhile the first of the scaling party who had got up, after taking both the towers and putting the sentinels to the sword, posted themselves inside to prevent anyone coming through against them. Rearing ladders from the wall, they sent several men up onto the towers, and from their summit and base kept in check, with their missiles, all the enemy who came up. Their main body planted a number of ladders against the wall, knocked down the battlements, and crossed over between the towers. Each man, as soon as he had got over, took up his station at the edge of the ditch and from there shot arrows and darts at any who came along the wall to stop the passage of his comrades. When all were over, the party on the towers came down, the last of them not without difficulty, and proceeded to the ditch, just as the three hundred came up carrying torches. The Plataeans, standing on the edge of the ditch in the dark, had a good view of their opponents and discharged their arrows and darts at the unarmed parts of their bodies, while they themselves could not be seen so well in the gloom because of the torches. Thus even the last of them got over the ditch, though not without effort and difficulty: ice had formed in it, not strong enough to walk on, but of the watery kind that generally comes with a wind more east than north, and the snow this wind had brought during the night had made the water in the ditch rise, so that they could scarcely breast it as they crossed. It was mainly the violence of the storm that allowed them to escape at all.

Starting from the ditch, the Plataeans went all together along the road leading to Thebes, keeping the chapel of the hero Androcrates on their right, on the principle that the last road the Peloponnesians would suspect them of taking would be the one toward their enemies’ country. Indeed they could see the pursuers with torches on the Athens road toward Cithaeron and Druoskephalai, or Oakheads. After going a little more than half a mile along the Thebes road, the Plataeans turned off and took the road leading to the mountain, to Erythrae and Hysiae, and reaching the hills made good their escape to Athens, two hundred and twelve men in all. Some had turned back into the town before getting over the wall, and one archer was taken prisoner at the outer ditch. The Peloponnesians meanwhile gave up the pursuit and returned to their posts. The Plataeans in the town, knowing nothing of what had happened, and informed by those who had turned back that not a single man had escaped, sent out a herald as soon as it was day to make a truce for the recovery of the dead bodies; then, learning the truth, they desisted. In this way the Plataean party got over and were saved.

Toward the close of the same winter, Salaethus, a Lacedaemonian, was sent out in a galley from Lacedaemon to Mitylene. Going by sea to Pyrrha, and from there overland, he passed along the bed of a torrent where the line of circumvallation could be crossed, and so entered Mitylene unnoticed and told the magistrates that Attica would certainly be invaded, and the forty ships intended to relieve them would arrive, and that he had been sent on to announce this and to oversee matters generally. The Mitylenians on this took courage and gave up the idea of treating with the Athenians. So this winter ended, and with it the fourth year of the war that Thucydides was the historian of.

The next summer the Peloponnesians sent off the forty-two ships for Mitylene, under Alcidas, their high admiral, while they themselves and their allies invaded Attica—their object being to distract the Athenians by a double movement, and so make it harder for them to act against the fleet sailing to Mitylene. The commander in this invasion was Cleomenes, in place of King Pausanias, son of Pleistoanax, his nephew, who was still a minor. Not content with laying waste whatever had grown back in the parts they had previously devastated, the invaders now extended their ravages to lands passed over in earlier incursions; so this invasion was felt by the Athenians more severely than any except the second. The enemy stayed on and on until they had overrun most of the country, expecting to hear from Lesbos of something achieved by their fleet, which they thought must by now have got across. However, since they did not get any of the results they expected, and their provisions began to run short, they retreated and dispersed to their various cities.

Meanwhile the Mitylenians, finding their provisions failing, while the fleet from the Peloponnese was loitering on the way instead of appearing at Mitylene, were forced to come to terms with the Athenians in the following way. Salaethus had himself ceased to expect the fleet to arrive, and now armed the commons with heavy armour, which they had not had before, intending to make a sortie against the Athenians. As soon as the commons found themselves possessed of arms, however, they refused to obey their officers any longer; and forming in groups, they told the authorities to bring out the provisions in public and divide them among them all, or they would themselves come to terms with the Athenians and surrender the city.

The government, aware of their inability to prevent this and of the danger they would face if left out of the capitulation, publicly agreed with Paches and the army to surrender Mitylene at discretion and admit the troops into the town, on the condition that the Mitylenians be allowed to send an embassy to Athens to plead their case, and that Paches should not imprison, enslave, or put to death any of the citizens until its return. Such were the terms of the capitulation; in spite of them, the chief authors of the negotiation with Lacedaemon were so completely overcome with terror when the army entered that they went and seated themselves by the altars, from which they were raised up by Paches under his promise to do them no wrong, and lodged at Tenedos until he should learn the will of the Athenians regarding them. Paches also sent some galleys and seized Antissa, and took such other military measures as he thought best.

Meanwhile the Peloponnesians in the forty ships, who should have made all haste to relieve Mitylene, lost time in coming round the Peloponnese itself, and continuing leisurely on the rest of the voyage made Delos without being seen by the Athenians at Athens. From there they reached Icarus and Myconus, where they first heard of the fall of Mitylene. Wishing to be sure of the truth, they put into Embatum, in the Erythraeid, about seven days after the capture of the town. There they learned the truth, and began to consider what they were to do. Teutiaplus, an Elean, addressed them as follows:

“Alcidas and Peloponnesians who share with me the command of this armament, my advice is to sail just as we are to Mitylene, before we have been heard of. We may expect to find the Athenians as much off their guard as men generally are who have just taken a city: this will certainly be true at sea, where they have no idea of any enemy attacking them, and where our strength happens chiefly to lie; while even their land forces are probably scattered through the houses in the carelessness of victory. So if we were to fall on them suddenly and at night, I have hopes, with the help of any well-wishers we may have left inside the town, that we shall master the place. Let us not shrink from the risk; let us remember that this is just the kind of occasion for one of the baseless panics common in war—and that to be able to guard against these in one’s own case, and to detect the moment when an attack will catch an enemy at this disadvantage, is what makes a successful general.”

These words of Teutiaplus failed to move Alcidas. Some of the Ionian exiles and the Lesbians with the expedition then began to urge him, since this seemed too dangerous, to seize one of the Ionian cities or the Aeolic town of Cyme, to use as a base for effecting the revolt of Ionia. This was by no means a hopeless venture, since their coming was welcome everywhere; their object would be to deprive Athens of her chief source of revenue, and at the same time to saddle her with expense if she chose to blockade them; and they would probably induce Pissuthnes to join them in the war. But Alcidas gave this proposal as bad a reception as the other, being eager—since he had come too late for Mitylene—to find himself back in the Peloponnese as soon as possible.

Accordingly he put out from Embatum and proceeded along shore, and touching at the Teian town of Myonnesus, butchered most of the prisoners he had taken on his passage. On coming to anchor at Ephesus, envoys came to him from the Samians at Anaia and told him that he was not going the right way to free Hellas by massacring men who had never raised a hand against him, and who were not enemies of his but allies of Athens against their will; and that if he did not stop, he would turn many more friends into enemies than enemies into friends. Alcidas agreed, and let go all the Chians still in his hands and some of the others he had taken. The inhabitants, instead of fleeing at the sight of his vessels, were rather coming up to them, taking them for Athenian, having no expectation that while the Athenians commanded the sea, Peloponnesian ships would venture over to Ionia.

From Ephesus Alcidas set sail in haste, and fled. He had been seen by the Salaminian and Paralian galleys, which happened to be sailing from Athens, while still at anchor off Clarus. Fearing pursuit, he now made across the open sea, fully determined to touch nowhere if he could help it until he reached the Peloponnese. Meanwhile news of him had reached Paches from the Erythraeid, and indeed from all quarters. As Ionia was unfortified, there were great fears that the Peloponnesians coasting along, even if they did not mean to stay, might make descents in passing and plunder the towns. Now the Paralian and Salaminian, having seen him at Clarus, brought the news themselves. Paches accordingly gave hot chase, and continued the pursuit as far as the island of Patmos. Then, finding that Alcidas had got too far ahead to be overtaken, he came back. He thought it fortunate that, since he had not encountered them out at sea, he had not overtaken them anywhere they would have been forced to encamp, giving him the trouble of blockading them.

On his way back along shore, he touched at, among other places, Notium, the port of Colophon, where the Colophonians had settled after the upper town was captured by Itamenes and the barbarians—who had been called in by certain individuals in a party quarrel. The capture of the town took place about the time of the second Peloponnesian invasion of Attica. The refugees, after settling at Notium, again split into factions, one of which called in Arcadian and barbarian mercenaries from Pissuthnes and, entrenching them in a quarter apart, formed a new community with the Median party of the Colophonians who had joined them from the upper town. Their opponents had retired into exile and now called in Paches, who invited Hippias, the commander of the Arcadians in the fortified quarter, to a parley, on condition that, if they could not agree, he would be put back safe and sound in the fortification. However, when Hippias came out to him, he put him in custody, though not in chains, and suddenly attacked and took by surprise the fortification, putting the Arcadians and the barbarians found inside it to the sword. Afterwards he took Hippias into it as he had promised, and, as soon as he was inside, seized him and shot him down. Paches then handed Notium over to the Colophonians not of the Median party; settlers were afterwards sent out from Athens, and the place was colonised under Athenian laws, after collecting all the Colophonians found in any of the cities.

Arrived at Mitylene, Paches reduced Pyrrha and Eresus; and finding the Lacedaemonian Salaethus in hiding in the town, sent him off to Athens, along with the Mitylenians he had placed in Tenedos, and any other persons he thought involved in the revolt. He also sent back the greater part of his forces, remaining with the rest to settle Mitylene and the rest of Lesbos as he thought best.

On the arrival of the prisoners with Salaethus, the Athenians at once put the latter to death, although he offered, among other things, to procure the withdrawal of the Peloponnesians from Plataea, which was still under siege. After deliberating about what to do with the others, in the fury of the moment they decided to put to death not only the prisoners at Athens but the entire adult male population of Mitylene, and to enslave the women and children. It was remarked that Mitylene had revolted without being subjected to the empire like the rest; and what most swelled the wrath of the Athenians was the fact that the Peloponnesian fleet had ventured over to Ionia to support her, a fact taken to argue a long-meditated rebellion. They accordingly sent a galley to communicate the decree to Paches, with orders to lose no time in dispatching the Mitylenians. The next day brought repentance with it, and reflection on the horrid cruelty of a decree that condemned a whole city to the fate deserved only by the guilty. As soon as the Mitylenian ambassadors at Athens and their Athenian supporters perceived this, they moved the authorities to put the question to the vote again. The authorities consented all the more readily because they could plainly see that most of the citizens wanted someone to give them the chance to reconsider. An assembly was therefore at once called, and after much expression of opinion on both sides, Cleon, son of Cleaenetus—the same man who had carried the previous motion to put the Mitylenians to death, the most violent man at Athens and at that time by far the most powerful with the commons—came forward again and spoke as follows:

“I have often before now been convinced that a democracy is incapable of empire, and never more so than by your present change of mind in the matter of Mitylene. Fears or plots being unknown in your daily relations with each other, you feel just the same toward your allies, and never reflect that the mistakes into which you may be led by listening to their appeals or by giving way to your own compassion are full of danger to yourselves, and bring you no thanks for your weakness from your allies. You entirely forget that your empire is a despotism and your subjects disaffected conspirators, whose obedience is ensured not by your suicidal concessions but by the superiority given you by your own strength, not by their loyalty. The most alarming feature in the case is the constant change of measures with which we appear to be threatened, and our seeming ignorance of the fact that bad laws which are never changed are better for a city than good ones that have no authority; that unlearned loyalty is more useful than quick-witted insubordination; and that ordinary men usually manage public affairs better than their more gifted fellows. The latter are always wanting to appear wiser than the laws, and to overrule every proposal brought forward, thinking they cannot show their wit on more important matters, and by this behaviour too often ruin their country. Those who mistrust their own cleverness are content to be less learned than the laws, and less able to pick holes in the speech of a good speaker; and being fair judges rather than rival athletes, they generally manage affairs successfully. We ought to imitate them, instead of being led on by cleverness and intellectual rivalry into giving advice contrary to our real opinions.

“For myself, I hold to my former opinion, and I am amazed at those who have proposed to reopen the case of the Mitylenians, and who are thus causing a delay that favours only the guilty—by making the sufferer proceed against the offender with the edge of his anger blunted; whereas vengeance, when it follows most closely upon the wrong, best matches it and most amply requites it. I wonder, too, who will be the man who maintains the contrary, and pretends to show that the crimes of the Mitylenians are useful to us, and our misfortunes injurious to the allies. Such a man must clearly either have such confidence in his rhetoric as to venture to argue that what has once been finally decided is still undetermined, or be bribed to try to delude us by elaborate sophisms. In such contests the state gives the rewards to others and takes the dangers for herself. The persons to blame are you, who are foolish enough to institute these contests; who go to see an oration as you would go to see a show; take your facts on hearsay; judge the practicability of a project by the wit of its advocates; trust for the truth about past events not to the fact you saw but to the clever criticisms you heard. You are easy victims of new-fangled arguments, unwilling to follow received conclusions; slaves to every new paradox, despisers of the commonplace; the first wish of every man being that he could speak himself, the next to rival those who can by seeming quite up with their ideas, applauding every hit almost before it is made, and being as quick to catch an argument as you are slow to foresee its consequences. You ask, if I may say so, for something different from the conditions under which we live, and yet you grasp those very conditions inadequately—true slaves to the pleasure of the ear, more like the audience of a rhetorician than the council of a city.

“To keep you from this, I proceed to show that no single state has ever injured you as much as Mitylene. I can make allowance for those who revolt because they cannot bear our empire, or who are forced to do so by the enemy. But for those who possessed an island with fortifications, who could fear our enemies only by sea—and there had their own force of galleys to protect them—who were independent and held in the highest honour by you—to act as these have done is not revolt; revolt implies oppression. It is deliberate and wanton aggression; an attempt to ruin us by siding with our bitterest enemies; a worse offence than a war undertaken on their own account in pursuit of power. The fate of those neighbours of theirs who had already rebelled and been subdued was no lesson to them; their own prosperity could not dissuade them from facing danger. Blindly confident in the future, with hopes beyond their power though not beyond their ambition, they declared war and chose to prefer might to right, their attack determined not by provocation but by the moment that seemed favourable. The truth is that great good fortune, coming suddenly and unexpectedly, tends to make a people insolent. In most cases it is safer for mankind to have success in reason than out of reason; and it is easier, one may say, to stave off adversity than to preserve prosperity. Our mistake has been to single out the Mitylenians as we have done: had they been treated long ago like the rest, they would never have so far forgotten themselves, since human nature is as surely made arrogant by consideration as it is awed by firmness. Let them now therefore be punished as their crime requires, and do not, while you condemn the aristocracy, absolve the people. This much is certain: all of them attacked you without distinction, although they might have come over to us and would now be back in possession of their city. But no, they thought it safer to throw in their lot with the aristocracy and joined their rebellion. Consider therefore: if you subject to the same punishment the ally who is forced to rebel by the enemy and the one who does so by his own free choice, which of them, do you suppose, will not rebel on the slightest pretext, when the reward of success is freedom and the penalty of failure nothing so very terrible? We meanwhile shall have to risk our money and our lives against one state after another; and if successful, we shall receive a ruined town from which we can no longer draw the revenue on which our strength depends; while if unsuccessful, we shall have one more enemy on our hands, and shall spend the time that might be used in fighting our existing foes in fighting our own allies.

“No hope, then, that rhetoric may instil or money purchase, of mercy due to human weakness, must be held out to the Mitylenians. Their offence was not involuntary, but malicious and deliberate; and mercy is for unwilling offenders alone. I therefore, now as before, persist against your reversing your first decision, or giving way to the three failings most fatal to empire—pity, sentiment, and indulgence. Compassion is due to those who can return the feeling, not to those who will never pity us in return, but are our natural and necessary foes. The orators who charm us with sentiment may find other, less important arenas for their talents than one in which the city pays a heavy penalty for a moment’s pleasure, while they receive fine compliments for their fine phrases. Indulgence should be shown toward those who will be our friends in future, not toward men who will remain just what they were, and as much our enemies as before. To sum up briefly, I say that if you take my advice you will do what is just toward the Mitylenians, and at the same time expedient; while by a different decision you will not so much oblige them as pass sentence on yourselves. For if they were right in rebelling, you must be wrong in ruling. However, if, right or wrong, you are determined to rule, then you must carry out your principle and punish the Mitylenians as your interest requires; or else you must give up your empire and cultivate honesty without danger. Make up your minds, then, to give them like for like; and do not let the victims who escaped the plot prove more insensible than the conspirators who hatched it. Reflect what they would have done to you if they had won—especially since they were the aggressors. It is those who wrong their neighbour without cause that hunt their victim to death, on account of the danger they foresee in letting their enemy survive; since the object of a wanton wrong is more dangerous, if he escapes, than an enemy who has not this to complain of. Do not, therefore, be traitors to yourselves, but call back as nearly as possible the moment of suffering and the supreme importance you then attached to their reduction; and now pay them back in their turn, without yielding to present weakness or forgetting the peril that once hung over you. Punish them as they deserve, and teach your other allies, by a striking example, that the penalty of rebellion is death. Once they understand this, you will not so often have to neglect your enemies while fighting with your own confederates.”

Such were the words of Cleon. After him Diodotus, son of Eucrates, who in the previous assembly had also spoken most strongly against putting the Mitylenians to death, came forward and spoke as follows:

“I do not blame those who have reopened the case of the Mitylenians, nor do I approve the protests we have heard against important questions being frequently debated. I think the two things most opposed to good counsel are haste and passion: haste usually goes hand in hand with folly, passion with coarseness and narrowness of mind. As for the argument that speech ought not to be the exponent of action, the man who uses it must be either senseless or interested—senseless if he believes it possible to deal with the uncertain future through any other medium; interested if, wishing to carry a disgraceful measure and doubting his ability to speak well in a bad cause, he thinks to frighten his opponents and his hearers by well-aimed slander. What is still more intolerable is to accuse a speaker of putting on a display in order to be paid for it. If only ignorance were imputed, an unsuccessful speaker might retire with a reputation for honesty, if not for wisdom; while the charge of dishonesty makes him suspected if successful, and thought, if defeated, not only a fool but a rogue. The city is no gainer by such a system, since fear deprives it of its advisers; though in truth, if our speakers are to make such accusations, it would be better for the country if they could not speak at all, since we would then make fewer blunders. The good citizen ought to triumph not by frightening his opponents but by beating them fairly in argument; and a wise city, without overdistinguishing its best advisers, will not deprive them of their due either, and, far from punishing an unlucky counsellor, will not even regard him as disgraced. In this way successful orators would be least tempted to sacrifice their convictions to popularity in the hope of still higher honours, and unsuccessful speakers least tempted to resort to the same popular arts in order to win over the multitude.

“This is not our way; and besides, the moment a man is suspected of giving advice, however good, from corrupt motives, we feel such a grudge against him for the gain we are not even sure he will receive that we deprive the city of its certain benefit. Plain good advice has thus come to be no less suspect than bad; and the advocate of the most monstrous measures is no more obliged to use deceit to gain the people than the best counsellor is to lie in order to be believed. The city—and the city only—because of these refinements, can never be served openly and without disguise; he who serves it openly is always suspected of serving himself in some secret way in return. Still, considering the magnitude of the interests involved and the position of affairs, we orators must make it our business to look a little farther than you, who judge offhand—especially as we, your advisers, are responsible, while you, our audience, are not. For if those who gave the advice and those who took it suffered equally, you would judge more calmly. As it is, you visit the disasters into which the whim of the moment may have led you on the single person of your adviser, not on yourselves, his many companions in error.

“However, I have not come forward either to oppose or to accuse in the matter of Mitylene. The question before us, as sensible men, is not their guilt but our interests. Even if I prove them ever so guilty, I shall not therefore advise their death unless it is expedient; nor, even if they have claims to indulgence, shall I recommend it unless it is clearly for the good of the country. I consider that we are deliberating for the future more than for the present; and where Cleon is so positive about the useful deterrent effects that will follow from making rebellion capital, I, who consider the interests of the future as much as he, just as positively maintain the contrary. I ask you not to reject my useful considerations for his specious ones. His speech may have the appeal of seeming the more just in your present temper against Mitylene; but we are not in a court of justice; we are in a political assembly. The question is not justice, but how to make the Mitylenians useful to Athens.

“Now of course communities have enacted the death penalty for many offences far lighter than this; still, hope leads men to take risks, and no one yet ever put himself in peril without the inward conviction that he would succeed. Again, was there ever a city rebelling that did not believe it possessed, either in itself or in its alliances, resources adequate to the enterprise? All—states and individuals alike—are prone to err, and there is no law that will prevent them. Or why should men have exhausted the list of punishments in search of measures to protect themselves from evildoers? It is probable that in early times the penalties for the greatest offences were less severe, and that, as these were disregarded, the death penalty has been arrived at by degrees in most cases—and is itself disregarded just the same. Either then some means of terror more terrible than this must be discovered, or it must be admitted that this restraint is useless; and that as long as poverty gives men the courage of necessity, or wealth fills them with the ambition that belongs to insolence and pride, and the other conditions of life keep each man under the thraldom of some fatal and master passion, so long the impulse will never be wanting to drive men into danger. Hope and cupidity—the one leading and the other following, the one conceiving the attempt, the other suggesting the ease of success—cause the widest ruin; though invisible agents, they are far stronger than the dangers seen. Fortune, too, powerfully helps the delusion, and by the unexpected aid she sometimes lends, tempts men to venture with inferior means. This is especially the case with communities, because the stakes played for are the highest—freedom or empire—and, when all are acting together, each man irrationally exaggerates his own capacity. In short, it is impossible, and only great simplicity can hope, to prevent human nature from doing what it has once set its mind upon, by force of law or by any other deterrent force whatsoever.

“We must not, therefore, commit ourselves to a false policy through belief in the efficacy of the death penalty, or shut rebels out from the hope of repentance and an early atonement for their error. Consider for a moment. At present, if a city that has already revolted sees that it cannot succeed, it will come to terms while it is still able to refund expenses and pay tribute afterwards. In the other case, what city, do you think, would not prepare better than is now done, and hold out to the last against besiegers, if it is all one whether it surrenders late or soon? And how can it be anything but harmful to us to be put to the expense of a siege, because surrender is out of the question; and—if we take the city—to receive a ruined town from which we can no longer draw the revenue that is our real strength against the enemy? We must not, then, sit as strict judges of offenders, to our own prejudice; rather we must see how, by moderate punishments, we can in future benefit from the revenue-producing powers of our dependencies. We must make up our minds to look for our protection not to legal terrors but to careful administration. At present we do exactly the opposite. When a free community, held in subjection by force, rises—as is only natural—and asserts its independence, no sooner is it reduced than we feel obliged to punish it severely; though the right course with free men is not to chastise them rigorously when they do rise, but to watch them rigorously before they rise and prevent them from ever conceiving the idea—and, once the insurrection is put down, to make as few responsible for it as possible.

“Only consider what a blunder you would commit by doing as Cleon recommends. As things stand, the people in all the cities is your friend, and either does not revolt with the oligarchy, or, if forced to do so, becomes at once the enemy of the insurgents; so that in the war with the hostile city you have the masses on your side. But if you butcher the people of Mitylene, who had nothing to do with the revolt, and who, as soon as they got arms, of their own accord surrendered the town, you will, first, commit the crime of killing your benefactors; and, second, play directly into the hands of the upper classes, who, when they induce their cities to rise, will at once have the people on their side—because you will have announced in advance the same punishment for those who are guilty and for those who are not. On the contrary, even if they were guilty, you should pretend not to notice it, in order to avoid alienating the only class still friendly to us. In short, I consider it far more useful for the preservation of our empire voluntarily to put up with injustice than to put to death, however justly, those whom it is in our interest to keep alive. As for Cleon’s idea that in punishment the claims of justice and expediency can both be satisfied, the facts do not confirm the possibility of such a combination.

“Confess, then, that this is the wisest course, and—without conceding too much either to pity or to indulgence (by neither of which motives do I, any more than Cleon, want you to be influenced)—be persuaded by me, on the plain merits of the case before you, to try calmly those of the Mitylenians whom Paches sent off as guilty, and to leave the rest undisturbed. This is at once best for the future and most terrifying to your enemies at the present moment, since good policy against an adversary is superior to the blind attacks of brute force.”

Such were the words of Diodotus. The two opinions thus expressed contradicted each other most directly; and the Athenians, despite their change of feeling, now proceeded to a vote, in which the show of hands was almost equal, although the motion of Diodotus carried the day. Another galley was at once sent off in haste, for fear that the first might reach Lesbos in the interval and the city be found destroyed; the first ship had about a day and a night’s start. Wine and barley-cakes were provided for the vessel by the Mitylenian ambassadors, and great promises made if they arrived in time. This caused the men to use such diligence on the voyage that they took their meals of barley-cakes kneaded with oil and wine while rowing, sleeping only by turns while the others were at the oar. Luckily they met no contrary wind, and the first ship made no haste on so horrid an errand, while the second pressed on as described. The first arrived only just before them, with Paches having only had time to read the decree and prepare to carry out the sentence, when the second put into port and prevented the massacre. The danger to Mitylene had indeed been great.

The other party whom Paches had sent off as the prime movers of the rebellion were, on Cleon’s motion, put to death by the Athenians, the number being rather more than a thousand. The Athenians also demolished the walls of the Mitylenians and took possession of their ships. Afterwards no tribute was imposed on the Lesbians; but all their land, except that of the Methymnians, was divided into three thousand allotments, three hundred of which were reserved as sacred for the gods, and the rest assigned by lot to Athenian shareholders, who were sent out to the island. With these the Lesbians agreed to pay a rent of two minae a year for each allotment, and cultivated the land themselves. The Athenians also took possession of the towns on the mainland belonging to the Mitylenians, which thus became for the future subject to Athens. Such were the events that took place at Lesbos.
